Name: Shaylee Rademacher
Badge: Teacher as Researcher | Sustaining Literacy Routines
Looking back on this inquiry cycle, what did you learn about your teaching and your students that you might not have noticed otherwise? How did engaging in this teacher-research process shape or shift your thinking about your classroom practice?:

I have learned that I don't know how to teach writing. I've been doing a lot of quickwrites and free writes in our writers' notebooks, but to go beyond that, I need my own training. I do see the value in what I've been doing, because they do buckle down and write when I ask them to, so that's good. I didn't share this in the discussion posts because I do not want to place blame, but I have a good friend of mine who is the 7th grade ELA teacher. I asked her if the students (we have the same students) had written argument paragraphs or papers. I thought that I could refer to this in my class, just to give them a reference point in their mind. She said they have not. She's retiring this year, and I'll miss her for many wonderful things she does, but it will be nice to partner with a new teacher so that we can build on the Layered Reading strategy.

I'm looking forward to continuing these classroom practices next year, especially the Say-Mean-Matter. I think if I had reviewed this strategy with my students before writing the argument for Fast Fashion, they may have better understood what I was looking for in an argument. I would like to do my own research into teaching argumentative writing this summer and hit the ground running next school year.

Think back to a moment during the lesson sequence that stands out. It could be a comment from a student, an unexpected challenge or success, a shift in engagement, or a moment when your own thinking changed. Describe what happened and why this moment feels meaningful to you now. What does it reveal:
All year I have truly been amazed by my students and how focused they are with their writing. Through this lesson sequence on Fast Fashion I was amazed by how focused they were with the long reading texts. The articles were multiple pages long, but I heard very few complaints. I bragged on them before hand, reminding them that we've been working on reading longer and longer non-fiction articles all year. I reminded them that like training for running in track, in which many of them are participating, we've been building their reading stamina. It seems to have worked. They read with hi-lighters in hand and did the close reading so well. It's a good feeling to look around a silent room at 18-24 students focused on reading. As a 7th grade science teacher I have the great joy of not MAP testing in science my year, but I do feel a responsibility to teach my content well so that they will perform well on the 8th grade science MAP test. With this literacy program I feel that I am making more of a contribution, especially for ELA, with building reading stamina and teaching reading strategies that will help in all areas. Ultimately, it's not about a state test, but developing lifelong readers, and thinkers; basically adults who can express themselves intelligently in their future.
As you look over the drafts your students produced in this lesson sequence, what early patterns, surprises, or questions are emerging for you? What aspects of your students’ writing are you most curious to explore more deeply with colleagues during our April regroup? What, if any, questions do you h:
They need a lot of work. After reading through some of them I've noticed that they need help with transitions. Since then we did an argumentative writing to support the claim, "My Spring break was the best ever because..." They used a description of great things they did to support their claim. I felt like this was good practice, and pretty to clear to them what was meant by evidence that supports the claim. I think it would be valuable for myself to learn basic transition words, and sentence start phrases that I can share with my students to help scaffold their writing process. I can't think of any questions at this time. Thank you, Julie!
